    • Market structure

    The market cycle and its emotions

    Large price moves often go through similar phases: accumulation, markup, distribution and markdown. Each phase comes with a dominant emotion among participants; from disbelief to euphoria, and from there to panic and depression. This scheme is a framework for thinking about which phase price may be in on the big picture.

    What is the market cycle?

    Price is the result of buyers' and sellers' decisions, and behind decisions are emotions such as expectation, fear and greed. That is why large rises and falls often move in a similar order, with similar emotions dominating each phase.

    The common scheme lists the emotions of a rise and the fall that follows it. It does not always play out the same way, but it is a useful language for reading the crowd's behaviour.

    Four phases

    The phases are read together with market structure.

    1. Accumulation After a decline price moves sideways for a while. No new low comes, or new lows stay as sweeps. Interest is low and the news is negative.
    2. Markup Price moves above the range and higher highs and higher lows (HH / HL) follow one another. Participation and volume grow.
    3. Distribution At the end of the rise price moves sideways again. New highs stay short or stay as sweeps. Interest and optimism are at their highest.
    4. Markdown Price moves below the range and lower highs and lower lows (LH / LL) follow one another. Selling speeds up, and in the end a new accumulation phase is reached.

    Emotions on the way up

    • Disbelief: the first rise from the bottom is not trusted; "this will fade like the previous recoveries".
    • Hope and optimism: a recovery starts to seem possible.
    • Belief and thrill: the rise is accepted; participation grows and the use of leverage spreads.
    • Euphoria: everyone thinks they are winning; risk is ignored most in this phase.

    Emotions on the way down

    • Complacency: the first drop is seen as a temporary pause.
    • Anxiety and denial: the drop lasts longer than expected, but the change of direction is not accepted.
    • Panic and capitulation: selling speeds up; positions are closed at any price.
    • Anger and depression: price moves sideways at the bottom and interest fades. The cycle starts again with disbelief.

    How is the scheme read?

    A common observation: the place of highest euphoria is often close to the top, and the place of deepest pessimism close to the bottom. Emotion does not show where price is going, but how far the crowd is crowded onto one side.

    The same order can show up at different scales: a large cycle on the monthly chart and a small wave on the hourly chart can go through similar phases. On a small scale, though, emotions last much shorter and the scheme works more loosely.

    What it shows, what it does not prove

    What it shows

    • A framework for the phases a large move can go through
    • The crowd behaviour that comes with price movement
    • Where the sideways phases (accumulation, distribution) sit between trends

    What it does not prove

    • Which phase the market is in right now; phases are often clear only in hindsight
    • How long the phases will last or how large they will be
    • That every cycle will follow this order in full

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    On MarketLevelMap the cycle's phases can be followed with structure marks.

    • The current direction (up, down, undetermined) and the BOS labels in the Price Action view show the consecutive breaks of the markup and markdown phases.
    • Accumulation and distribution often show up on the chart as a sideways market. The range (RH, EQ, RL) and the sweep labels in the same view are one way to follow these phases.

    In crypto

    Because crypto trades 24/7 and leverage is common, the phases can play out fast and hard; the panic and capitulation phases in particular can be squeezed into a few hours by sudden liquidations.

    Often confused with

    • Ranges and consolidationAccumulation and distribution are both sideways markets; they differ in their place in the cycle, accumulation after a decline, distribution after a rise.
    • What is a trend?A trend describes price's direction; the cycle describes the large-scale order of trends and the sideways phases between them.

    Key points

    • Large moves often go through accumulation, markup, distribution and markdown.
    • Each phase comes with a dominant emotion; euphoria is close to the top, pessimism close to the bottom.
    • The phases are often clear only in hindsight.
    • The scheme is not a timing tool but a framework for reading the crowd.
